newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Klima will accept "highest offer" for CA.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Klima will accept "highest offer" for CA.

text.p: Austrian Finance Minister Viktor Klima said on Tuesday he would decide on the sale of privatisation candidate Creditanstalt-Bankverein as soon as possible and would accept only the highest offer.
"It will happen as soon as possible," he told a news conference, adding: "I will accept the best and highest offer."
Klima last week extended the tender to January 10 from a previous December 16 deadline to allow the three bidders to spruce up their offers for Austria's blue-blooded bank.

"I will scrutinise the offers after they've landed on my desk at 9 a.m. (0800 GMT) on January 10 and I'm prepared to accept any offer that comes in above 16.7 billion schillings ($1.5 billion)," he said.
The highest bid is reported to have come from Bank Austria, which has bid 16.8 billion schillings for the government's 70 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt.

But the sale of the Alpine republic's second largest bank has veered from a straight privatisation into a quagmire of political gerrymandering that is threatening the survival of the year-old coalition government.
The two governing parties -- Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's Social Democrats (SPOe) and the conservative People's Party -- each back a separate bidder in the marathon Creditanstalt sale.
The conservatives have called for a special session of parliament on January 14 to debate the sale and have warned Klima against making any definitive decision before that.

Klima, bound by European Union law to sell the bank to the highest bidder, refused to be pinned down on whether he would decide before parliament meets but said: "I take it for granted that it won't take 10 days."
If he did take the decision before parliament meets, the creaky coalition could break apart.
While the Social Democrats back Bank Austria, controlled by the SPOe-dominated City of Vienna, the People's Party favour a bid by an international consortium grouped around insurer EA-Generali.
The two parties have entered a critical week with both parties holding separate congresses where they were expected to map out their divided opinions on how the bank should be sold.
People's Party leader and Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel on Tuesday presented his party's three options for the sale at his party congress in Goldegg, near Salzburg.
He above all supports the EA-Generali consortium bid, followed by a takeover of the core stake by institutional investors with the remaining shares widely spread.
A third solution would be to float the state's entire stake on the stock market, which analysts have said was a "economically unwise" solution.
Schuessel said he could only foresee a sale to Bank Austria if the City of Vienna withdraws fully from Bank Austria.
Bidders have until Friday to make their final offers.

The EA-Generali consortium has offered a total of 13.8 billion schillings for the state's 19.9 million shares in the bank and wants to sell about a quarter of those on the market at a premium, 60 percent of which would also go to the government's coffers.
The third offer made by Austrian entrepreneur and former retail magnate Karl Wlaschek has not been disclosed but is estimated at around 15 billion schillings. ($1=10.90 Schilling)
